[54] White Paper 2004 Analysis Balance Sheet

[55] Perspectives Foreword by the Federal Minister of Defence

[56] With the publication of its first White Paper, the Federal Ministry of Defence is embarking on a new path in security policy communication – at the national and international levels

[57] Based on the analysis of the security policy situation, the military strategic orientation and development of the Austrian Armed Forces are described and the perspectives for the coming years are presented

[58] This year, Austria celebrates the fiftieth anniversary of the decision to establish a sovereign army following the signing of the State Treaty in

[59] The end of the East-West conflict and the expansion of the EU and NATO have fundamentally changed the security policy framework for Austria

[60] This also entails massive changes in the tasks of the armed forces

[61] While national defense used to be the priority, international crisis management now tops the list of priorities

[62] The Austrian Armed Forces are therefore undergoing a transformation process aimed at developing the capabilities necessary to meet the increasing demands placed on modern armed forces in the 21st century

[63] The spectrum ranges from participation in military crisis management tasks to international conflict prevention and peacekeeping measures within the framework of the European Union, the United Nations, NATO/PfP or the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe

[64] The participation of the Austrian Armed Forces in the field of humanitarian aid and disaster relief as well as in the security police assistance mission at the Schengen external border must be taken into account

[65] Ensuring the capabilities for military protection of state sovereignty is the central prerequisite

[66] Austria’s security is inextricably linked to European security

[67] It is therefore necessary for Austria to participate actively in the further development and expansion of the European Security and Defence Policy

[68] It is in our own interest to help shape this policy area – only a corresponding commitment in the international area of security policy will lead to a role of “shaper” and prevent a passive stand-off

[69] The broad scope of this White Paper arises from the fact that this publication equally considers three essential factors: analysis, review and perspectives

[70] First, there is a comprehensive analysis of the international security situation, the new threats and risks, and the measures taken by the international community, which are also determining factors for the transformation process in the Austrian Armed Forces. This is followed by an assessment of the fulfilment of the Armed Forces' tasks, with a focus on the years 2003 and

[71] Finally, the transformation process is presented comprehensively, starting with the objectives of the Federal Army Reform Commission and its recommendations for the necessary reform steps

[72] This White Paper clearly indicates that the upcoming reform represents a decisive step towards Austria becoming a military instrument that will meet future challenges within the framework of a European security and defence policy and will have both the credible ability to protect the Austrian population and make a military contribution to the community of nations that corresponds to Austria's status

[73] To promote internal and external acceptance, a balance should be achieved between the required skills and the available resources

[74] This White Paper is aimed at the political public and those in positions of responsibility in order to improve understanding of security policy needs

[75] The soldiers of the Austrian Armed Forces can be proud of their achievements at home and internationally

[76] However, a country's defense policy is only sustainable if it is recognized as such by all citizens

[80] The term white paper: What is a white paper and what is it used for

[81] The different definitions of a white paper essentially have in common that it is a compilation of documents, statistics, reports, etc. on a specific policy area, which was prepared by a government agency and is presented to the public

[82] For example, White Papers of the European Commission contain proposals for Community action in a particular area

[83] They contain formal proposals for certain policy areas and serve to develop these areas

[84] They are not to be understood as legal acts, but rather as a basis for discussion

[85] The term itself comes from the color of the cover

[86] For example, there are also "Green Papers" from the European Commission. Framework and content

[120] Security situation 3.1.1 Security and security policy

[121] The term “security” has a broad meaning today and includes, among other things, individual (personal) security, security against health risks, workplace security, crime, terrorism, environmental pollution, fear of foreign infiltration, etc

[122] Security is often perceived subjectively and this does not correspond to objective (actual) security

[123] The more security is required, the lower the degree of individual and collective freedom that can be granted

[124] Based on Maslow's hierarchy of needs, the basic needs (food, survival guarantee) of around one billion people worldwide are not met

[125] The need for security (housing, work, protection from illness) remains unattainable for about two billion people

[126] Social needs (family, friendships, contacts in a socially regulated environment) are only superficially met

[127] The need for recognition and self-realization are only possible for a small group

[128] However, even in industrialized countries, security regarding the availability of basic needs and greater security is no longer guaranteed

[129] Security policy is a fundamental policy area of every state

[130] It is defined as the totality of political objectives, strategies and instruments that serve external security, state sovereignty and the freedom of action of the government, as well as the independence and political self-determination of a state

[131] Security policy is a cross-departmental, national task

[132] Their form makes clear what role a state is willing to play regionally and globally

[133] The task of defense policy as part of security policy is to ensure sovereignty and territorial integrity, the principles of democracy and the rule of law, and the protection of the life of the population and their property against external attack

[134] The security situation from a global perspective

[135] At the end of the 20th century, the international system supported by states changed fundamentally

[136] With the end of the Cold War, a basic pattern of possible orientation for states has disappeared, namely the communist variant of the order

[137] With the disappearance of the Second World, namely the Soviet-communist world, the division into the First, Second and Third World is no longer relevant

[138] Analysis of the balance sheet

[139] The generally defining characteristic of the current security situation is a decreasing predictability of its development

[140] The number of state and non-state actors operating across borders, some of whom have significant weight and impact in a wide range of policy areas in a globalized world, has increased considerably

[141] In addition, new centers of power of regional or material importance are emerging – both in the economic and technological development spheres, as well as in military terms

[142] These dynamic developments also create new interdependencies in security policy

[143] Since 1989, the stability achieved through the balance of power between the superpowers and through nuclear deterrence has been replaced by processes that are increasingly less controllable by state power

[144] The global dimension of security policy In world politics, despite the special position of the USA, a tendency towards regionalization and multipolarity is becoming noticeable

[145] The bipolar constellation of world politics has been and is increasingly being replaced by new structurally determining regional associations of varying importance, such as the European Union (EU), the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the South American Common Market (MERCOSUR), the North American Free Trade Area (NAFTA), the African Union (AU), the World Islamic Movement (OIC) and the Asia-Pacific Cooperation (APEC

[146] Multipolarization is also reflected in the emergence and rise of new regional powers

[147] Following the dissolution of the bipolar order, these regional powers, such as India, Nigeria and Brazil, are attempting to use their potential (such as population, territory, economic power and armed forces) to expand their own position towards regional supremacy in the sense of traditional power thinking

[148] This affects both the sovereignty of smaller states in the respective region and the interests of actors outside the region and harbors potential for conflict

[149] The number of actors relevant to security policy is increasing: ¾ through the increase in the number of states with different territorial size, political importance, economic capability or military power

[150] by the growth of the number of international organisations

[151] through the rapid increase in the number and importance of transnational social actors (non-governmental organizations/NGOs) that are active in the fields of global environmental protection, development work, human rights and humanitarian aid, among others, and through the increase in the number and importance of non-state-controlled, but transnationally effective actors that pursue independent economic, religious or ideological interests, possibly even by using violent means

[152] Due to the loss of the binding effects of the bipolar world order from the time of the East-West confrontation and the often insufficient stabilizing capacity of regional security organizations, the further development of relations between the individual actors and thus global development can no longer be predicted in the long term

[153] The number of states possessing weapons of mass destruction and suitable delivery systems is increasing

[154] The process of globalization is accelerating, particularly through the progressive development and consolidation of global market processes, global communication infrastructure, universal guiding principles and fundamental values, globally networked science and research, the emergence of global actor networks, etc

[155] States must adapt to these new conditions

[156] In general, the importance of the economy over the military in shaping international relations is increasing

[157] In an increasingly interconnected world, “national security” depends to a significant extent on the regional stability framework, and “regional security” is influenced by “global security”

[158] Cross-border risks, transnational dependencies and new technological developments as well as the increasing vulnerability of modern societies mean that zones of stability and instability cannot coexist without mutual influences

[159] Inevitably, instability will also spread to stable regions

[160] Spatial distance from conflict zones has long since ceased to provide sufficient protection in various respects

[161] White Paper 2004 Analysis Balance Sheet Perspectives

[162] The security situation in Europe

[163] Europe’s security situation has improved significantly since the end of the Cold War

[164] With the positive change in the geopolitical situation in the Eurostrategic zone, Austria's situation has also improved substantially

[165] From the Eurasian superpower

[166] According to experts, the Russian Federation does not pose a strategic-operational threat in the classic military sense to the European core zone and thus to Austria due to the drastic deterioration of its geopolitical situation caused by the ongoing expansion of the Euro-Atlantic zone, the growing US influence in the South Caucasus, Central Asia, Afghanistan and the Middle East, taking into account its foreign policy and economic objectives, the ongoing military reform and the associated long-term goal of reducing its armed forces

[167] The objective of the Russian armed forces reform is clearly defensive (state-preserving) and an integral part of the comprehensive security policy concept

[168] Remaining capabilities for power projection beyond Russian state borders Traditional dimensions and content of power have changed

[169] Particularly in the western industrialized countries, it is the technological and scientific foundations, the industrial and financial performance of an economy, the ability to enforce its own legal and value systems, and the control of knowledge and information that determine the power of a state

[170] Information and communication technology has acquired a unique significance within security policy because it links all other security policy dimensions and thus becomes an independent factor of power and influence

[171] With the exception of a few isolated areas, the global networking of information and communication technology has become a reality

[172] The enormous development problems of the less developed countries, whose inhabitants make up the majority of the world's population, harbor potential for conflict which, without appropriate conflict management, will lead to diverse conflict constellations and conflict resolutions whose intensity and impact are not yet foreseeable

[173] A particular risk potential is posed by the fact that all these processes have acquired a new quality and dimension due to the availability of new means, especially modern weapons systems

[174] Above all, highly developed information technology, the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, some of which are very easy and cheap to produce, and long-range delivery systems, as well as the most modern genetic engineering developments, which cannot yet be assessed, are opening up completely new possibilities for unpredictable state powers and non-state actors such as terrorist movements, organized crime groups, sects, but also individual perpetrators to achieve their goals

[175] States can only counter these dangers in international cooperation

[176] The number of armed conflicts has remained high

[177] Immediate negative effects of these largely intrastate conflicts, even on more stable states in the region, include forced mass migration and disruption of international economic trade

[178] In addition, these primarily intrastate conflicts, which are financed by their own "civil war economies" in the form of arms, drug, and human trafficking, can also have indirect destabilizing effects on neighboring societies and states

[179] This development is leading to an increasing willingness of international intervention to restabilise such conflict regions, including the use of military force

[180] Of fundamental relevance for the further development of the world of states and international relations will be population development, the distribution of energy and resources, nutritional problems, environmental damage, migration problems, and the interrelationships and conditions existing in these problem areas

[181] Perspectives will continue to shrink, but at the same time the ability to resolve conflicts within borders will increase

[182] In this context, the conflict in Chechnya in particular needs to be addressed, as the regions of Afghanistan, Iraq and Palestine will require increased military engagement by European states in these regions in the future

[183] Austria and its security policy environment With Austria's EU membership and the implementation of the EU treaties of Maastricht, Amsterdam and Nice, as well as the commitment made within the framework of the Helsinki Headline Goal (HHG), Austria's geopolitical and militarystrategic situation has changed in light of the developments in the European Security and Defence Policy (ESDP

[184] The national sphere of interest has thus been expanded to include that of the EU

[185] Thus, the crisis regions in and on the periphery of Europe (South-Eastern Europe, South Caucasus, Central Asia, Middle East and North Africa) are also becoming increasingly relevant for Austria in view of possible military operations within the framework of the ESDP

[186] The pressure on Austria to participate in future peace support operations (Peace Support for the Russian Federation) within the framework of European solidarity, in line with its economic strength and population size, also represents a challenge from a long-term perspective

[187] With the admission of new members to NATO and the EU in 2004, the European area of stability was expanded

[188] This situation does not indicate any threat to the territory of the EU Member States from conventional armed forces at present or in the foreseeable future

[189] This is a military consequence of the political overcoming of the division of the continent

[190] Nevertheless, Europe is not free from threats today

[191] Some of the causes lie within Europe, but some originate in far-away regions

[192] In addition to the calculable situation in Eastern and Central Europe, the current developments in Southeastern Europe with three acute crisis areas (Kosovo, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Macedonia) as well as the latent crisis potential on the European periphery (South Caucasus, Central Asia, North Africa and the Near/Middle East) with the acute conflicts White Paper 2004 Analysis Balance Sheet Perspectives Operations/PSO) is becoming increasingly greater

[193] Austria's commitment is also determined by Austria's political position within Europe and its specific objectives

[194] The end of the East-West conflict and the expansion of the EU and NATO have fundamentally changed the security policy framework for Austria

[195] There is no conventional military threat to our territory in the foreseeable future

[196] However, the effects of European and non-European instabilities as well as subconventional threats may continue to influence Austria's security in the future

[197] Main actors from an Austrian perspective Neighbouring countries

[198] The country structure of Central Europe is predominantly characterized by small states

[199] Austria is surrounded by eight neighboring countries, of which Germany and Italy are large states

[200] Of these eight countries

[201] Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Slovenia and Italy of both the European Union and NATO

[202] International Organizations European Union

[203] Before the historic turning point of 1989, Europe’s security was determined by the East-West conflict

[204] Pan-European stability was based on the “balance of terror” between the North Atlantic Alliance, led by the USA, and the Warsaw Pact, led by the Soviet Union

[205] The changes in 1989 created a completely new political situation in Europe

[206] It created a new security environment with a number of new risks and uncertainties

[207] The changes required an expansion of the political dimension of the European Community (EC

[208] Europe was confronted with the reality that it must assume greater responsibility both for safeguarding its own security and for stabilizing its environment

[209] The European Council therefore decided in Dublin in April 1990 to start work on Political Union in order to enable the EC to meet the requirements of the new circumstances effectively and efficiently

[210] The Union should not only have a foreign policy The only non-NATO and non-EU members border western Austria

[212] As the Swiss Federal Council stated in its "Security Policy Report 2000," the two traditional pillars of Swiss security policy—autonomous defense and neutrality—have lost much of their importance for maintaining security in Europe over the past decade

[214] Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP

[215] With the Single European Act (SEA) in February 1986, not only was the development of a common European internal market – an economy without internal borders – initiated, but it also gave a contractual and institutional basis to European Political Cooperation (EPC), which had been in practice since

[216] Due to the events in the former Yugoslavia and the military action of the international community against Iraq in response to its annexation of Kuwait, the development of the Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP) was initiated with the Dublin and Rome Summits in

[217] With the Treaty of Maastricht of 7 February 1992, the CFSP was established as the second intergovernmental

[218] The objectives of the CFSP include safeguarding the common values, fundamental interests and independence of the Union; strengthening the security of the Union and its Member States in all its forms; the maintenance of peace and the strengthening of international security in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations; the development and strengthening of democracy and the rule of law, as well as respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms

[219] The objectives of the CFSP include safeguarding the common values, fundamental interests and independence of the Union; strengthening the security of the Union and its Member States in all its forms

[220] the maintenance of peace and the strengthening of international security in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations

[221] the development and strengthening of democracy and the rule of law, as well as respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms

[222] The main substantive innovation compared to the EPC is the pronounced security policy component of the CFSP

[223] The CFSP now covers all areas of foreign and security policy, including the gradual establishment of a common defence policy, which could lead to a common defence if the European Council so decides

[224] This laid the foundation for today's European Security and Defence Policy (ESDP), which is a component of the CFSP

[225] The Treaty of Amsterdam of 2 October 1997 gave the CFSP new dynamism, increased visibility and coherence

[226] The following innovations should be noted: the instrument of the ‘Common Strategy’ in areas where Member States have important common interests

[227] ¾ the transfer of the so-called Petersberg tasks18 from the Western European Union (WEU) to the EU

[228] This will enable the EU to carry out military international crisis management

[229] — the creation of a ‘High Representative (Representative) for the CFSP’ (‘Mr. CFSP’), which is intended to increase the visibility of the Union’s CFSP

[230] — the creation of the Planning and Early Warning Unit within the Council Secretariat

[231] the possibility of appointing EU Special Representatives for specific political issues

[232] In the Maastricht and Amsterdam Treaties, the EU commits itself not only to the creation of this Common Foreign and Security Policy but also to the prospect of a common defence policy

[233] Likewise, in December 1997, the European Council in Luxembourg decided to enlarge the European Union

[234] On May 1, 2004, ten new countries were admitted

[235] The European Union now comprises 25 member states, 19 of which are also members of the North Atlantic Alliance

[236] On 16/17 June 2004, negotiations on the EU Constitutional Treaty were concluded, which was initialled by the heads of state and government of the 25 EU Member States in Rome on 29 October

[237] Due to planned ratifications in some member states, the EU Constitution is not expected to enter into force until the end of 2006 at the earliest

[238] What will then be new – in contrast to the Amsterdam Treaty in the Nice version – is the possibility of taking majority decisions in the area of the CFSP

[239] The new EU Treaty includes, among other things, closer cooperation in the area of mutual defence, an extension of the spectrum of Petersberg tasks, solidarity among EU Member States in the event of non-state terrorist attacks and natural disasters, and permanent structured cooperation, which provides for closer cooperation between EU Member States in the development of defence capabilities

[240] European Security and Defence Policy (ESDP

[241] The creation of the ESDP within the CFSP was initiated by the first Austrian EU Presidency, based on the British-French initiative of St. Malo in 1998 and the European Council in Vienna in the same year

[242] This resulted in the political declaration of intent of the Cologne European Council (4 June 1999) in the wake of the Kosovo conflict that “the Union must have the capacity for autonomous action, supported by credible military capabilities, as well as the means and willingness to decide on their use, in order to respond to international crisis situations, without prejudice to NATO action....”

[243] The ESDP essentially pursues the following objectives: Conflict prevention

[244] Promoting non-violent conflict resolution is a key concern of the EU

[245] White Paper 2004 Analysis Balance Sheet Perspectives

[246] Strengthening the transatlantic partnership: The EU and NATO/USA remain each other’s most important partners

[247] Both sides benefit from a Europe that is more capable of taking action thanks to ESDP capabilities

[248] Strengthening international organisations: The EU will use ESDP resources in accordance with the principles of the UN Charter and will be able to respond to requests from lead organisations such as the UN and the OSCE

[249] Crisis management: The core area of the ESDP is crisis management using military and civilian means

[250] A hallmark and particular strength of the ESDP is the parallel development of military and civilian capabilities

[251] On 11 December 1999, the European Council in Helsinki decided to build up its own military capacities for international crisis management

[252] Accordingly, armed forces of between 50,000 and 60,000 men were to be built up by 2003 to cover the entire Petersberg spectrum; the civilian resources (5,000 police officers, strengthening the rule of law, strengthening the administration and civil protection) were determined at the European Council in Feira in

[253] The European Council of December 2003 officially concluded the process initiated in Helsinki, although further efforts are still needed to achieve the European armed forces objectives

[254] At the same time, the Council adopted the European Security Strategy "A Secure Europe in a Better World", which contains guidelines for the further development of the CFSP and the ESDP

[255] Both developments together form the basis for the development of a new Headline Goal for the Armed Forces

[257] Common Security and Defence Policy (CSDP

[258] United Nations The principles and purposes of the UN are set out in the Charter of the UN, signed in San Francisco on 26 June 1945 and entered into force on 24 October

[259] Its primary objective is to maintain world peace and international security

[260] Further objectives according to Art

[261] of the Charter are: respect for human rights, international cooperation in the economic, cultural, social and humanitarian fields, including the protection of the environment, the development of friendly relations between the 191 member states

[262] In achieving these objectives, Member States must observe the principles set out in Article 2 of the Charter: - a general prohibition of the use of force and the obligation to settle disputes peacefully (except for the right of self-defence and legitimate coercive measures decided upon by the Security Council in accordance with Chapter VII of the Charter), - the principle of the sovereign equality of all Member States, - the prohibition of interference by the Organisation in the internal affairs of its members

[263] However, the scope of the states' "internal" affairs was increasingly restricted

[264] In particular, the protection of human rights is increasingly seen as less of an exclusively internal matter for a country

[265] The most important organ of the UN is the Security Council (UNSC), which has extensive powers in conflict prevention and resolution and is the only body that can make binding decisions for all UN members

[321] The Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) is the most comprehensive European security organization in the sense of cooperative security

[322] It emerged from the process initiated by the actual Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE, 1973-1975) and initially led to an increasingly dense network of conferences

[323] The transition to an actual organization began with the establishment of the first permanent institutions of the then CSCE at the Paris Summit in 1990 and was finally completed at the Budapest Summit in 1994 with the renaming of the already largely institutionalized CSCE to OSCE

[324] The OSCE differs significantly from other security policy institutions, such as the EU or NATO, in several ways

[330] In terms of content, the OSCE's focus is on developing long-term perspectives, particularly on creating rules that should enable peaceful coexistence in Europe

[363] Global Actors Today we find a system of domination in international relations that represents a mixture of a unipolar and a multipolar system

[364] From the perspective of security policy, the world today presents itself as a system of states and organizations that is shaped by the dominance of the USA

[365] In addition, there are a number of major powers that have achieved both regional and global importance

[366] In the following, three important global actors are briefly characterized

[367] The USA can pursue its national interests worldwide and, if necessary, enforce them militarily

[368] A strong economy, a leading position in research and development, a lead in many areas of high technology, and superior military potential – combined with a strong political willingness to act – form the basis of US supremacy

[369] Particularly important security policy objectives of the USA are to guarantee free access to strategic raw materials, to secure open markets for its economy and to maintain existing alliances

[370] The USA advocates for the global enforcement of democracy and human rights

[371] These interests also determine their engagement in the various regions of the world

[372] There is an increasing tendency towards a unilateral approach if necessary

[373] In the spirit of burden sharing, the United States aims to ensure that regional actors (regional powers allied with the United States or alliances led by the United States) assume more material responsibility for regional stabilization in the future

[374] At the same time, the aim is to prevent unpredictable states or states hostile to the USA from gaining power as regional powers

[375] Russian Federation Russia remains a major military power, particularly because of its possession of intercontinental nuclear weapons

[376] The majority of the political elites and parts of society still see themselves as committed to a claim to power based on the Soviet Union's role as a world power at the time and, due to widespread geopolitical thinking, sees a special role for Russia not only in the Eurasian region, but also as a major global player

[377] Russia's elites consider the borders with Europe to be the only truly secure ones

[378] Europe is also the largest provider of technology, management know-how, and investor

[379] In contrast, in the southern and southeastern regions, crisis situations are increasing for the continued territorial existence of the country

[380] Russia's strategic parity with the USA no longer exists today

[381] However, there is the possibility of a corresponding role in international relations, particularly in a foreign and alliance policy directed against the USA

[382] Cooperation with major regional powers in Asia, especially with China and India, therefore appears to be a realistic option for Russian foreign policy, at least in the medium term

[383] The People's Republic of China is a steadily gaining power in the Asia-Pacific region, characterized by continued population growth, a continuous economic upswing, and a long-term modernization of its armed forces

[384] These developments make China increasingly capable of regional power projection

[385] Because of the strong position of the central power, ethnic-religious or economically based internal tensions are unlikely to lead to explosive developments

[386] However, the increasingly strong contradiction between capitalist economic policy and communist-authoritarian social policy is unmistakable

[387] China's central security policy objectives are to establish and expand its dominant position in the Eastern Pacific region and, in the long term, to establish a strategic balance with the United States

[388] Chinese politics influences global development to a great extent, which in turn has repercussions for Europe and the European Union's options for action and relations in the pursuit of its interests, at least in the Eurasian region

[390] The collapse of communism in the Soviet Union and in the Eastern/Southeastern European countries since 1989/90, as well as the dissolution of the Warsaw Pact, also led to the abolition of a possible military confrontation between the two power blocs, the Warsaw Pact with the USSR at the forefront, and NATO, led by the USA

[391] The decline of a potential East-West conflict and the shift from a bipolar to a multipolar system have not led to a reduction, but rather to a change, in the global threat potential

[392] The reduction of spheres of influence of the two “superpowers” favored the emergence of numerous unstable zones and the reappearance of old ethnic, religious and historical fault lines (e.g. Balkans, Caucasus, Central Asia

[393] The Cold War provided a stable framework for decades

[394] Its end did not bring comprehensive peace, but rather created massive new problems

[395] The reorganization of the international system was not peaceful everywhere; numerous new, previously unknown and changing factors played a role

[396] Experts in the field of security policy have been pointing out the potential new threats in their analyses for many years, but their warnings were mostly laughed at and not taken seriously – until the terrorist attacks in the USA on September 11, 2001, with all their consequences

[397] The European Union and other Western countries are facing new security challenges

[398] Instead of a relatively clear and, above all, military-dominated threat picture, there has been a mutually influencing, difficult-to-calculate mixture of risks that may have their origin in the political, economic, military, social, cultural-religious, information and communication technology, or ecological dimensions

[399] A change in the nature of wars has been evident for several years

[400] As the boundaries between regular soldiers, irregular fighters, terrorists and criminals become blurred, the distinction between combatants and non-combatants, which has been essential in international law to date, also disappears

[401] What was created through centuries of effort in international law to protect the civilian population and to limit war is largely no longer relevant today

[402] The security policy changes of recent years have led to an increase in the importance of new forms of threat

[403] These include organized crime (OC), irregular migration, terrorism, weapons of mass destruction and their delivery systems (including relevant dual-use goods), the use of various missiles for terrorist purposes, and also forms of information warfare

[404] While the detection and combating of these phenomena was previously primarily the responsibility of the security executive, today the armed forces are increasingly involved as the security forces are becoming more and more overwhelmed

[405] In Austria and many other countries, support to combat these phenomena is usually provided in the form of administrative and security police assistance

[406] Within the framework of these assistance services, however, the armed forces are faced with completely new tasks outside the traditional military spectrum of tasks, which give rise to completely new, immediate dangers and threats for the soldiers deployed

[476] Weapons of mass destruction (WMD) and proliferation

[477] Currently, a number of states officially possess WMD and delivery systems

[478] However, the direct threat posed by these states is considered to be rather low, as they primarily view their WMD and delivery systems as a means of political pressure to enforce political and/or economic interests

[479] The number of states possessing WMD and corresponding delivery systems continues to increase despite existing agreements and non-proliferation measures

[480] This risk potential is exacerbated if such WMDs fall into the hands of violent non-state actors such as terrorist groups or organized crime

[481] A threat posed by WMD can therefore be divided into three sub-areas: - states that possess WMD and delivery systems, - proliferation of WMD and delivery systems, - terrorist organizations that acquire WMD

[579] The Austrian Armed Forces in Society 4.1 Armed Forces, Society and State in the Democratic Political System

[580] In democratic societies, the military represents a social subsystem that is functionally linked to society as a whole

[581] Society is to be understood as a system of action that produces all measures and institutions that ensure its own viability

[582] The state must also be seen as a part of society as a whole, namely as the element that is endowed with the power to maintain order and has the means of power at its disposal

[583] The military is part of this state monopoly on order and acts in the democratic context as an instrument of politics under the primacy of politics

[584] Through their existence and the manner in which they contribute to Austria's overall political interests within the European context, the Austrian Armed Forces contribute both in principle and in practice to Austrian sovereignty and the common good of the country as a whole

[585] The new security policy environment has brought about a drastic expansion of tasks for the Austrian Armed Forces in terms of internationalization and the perception of "new" challenges, which, while based on the ability to fulfill traditional military tasks, entail radical changes in terms of organizational structure, personnel and material requirements, and, last but not least, operational capabilities

[586] In an open democratic society, however, adequate performance by armed forces can only be achieved in the long term if a predominantly affirmative social environment exists

[587] Without the support of society, the military risks losing its material and ideological base

[588] Not least for this reason, in this age of paradigmatic changes in the area of state security, the greatest attention must be paid to raising socio-political awareness

[589] However, the newly created security policy framework takes the Austrian Armed Forces far beyond their previously dominant task of national defense and, through the new, demanding range of tasks, opens up new socio-politically relevant development opportunities for the Austrian Armed Forces

[590] Purpose of the military organization and positioning of the armed forces in society

[591] The military is linked to political developments and is part of a process of social rationalization

[592] In this context, the military is responsible for enforcing state objectives in the event of an armed conflict or other exceptional situations, such as disasters

[593] The primary function of the military is to ensure external security, although current developments are increasingly blurring the lines between external and internal security, making it impossible to distinguish them clearly

[594] This not only leads to new tasks for the armed forces within the framework of a comprehensively understood concept of security, but also to increased civil-military cooperation

[595] However, these radical changes are not yet widely recognized and acknowledged by the Austrian population or politicians

[596] The relationship between the military and society as a whole is essentially determined by the political system and social relations, which is why the armed forces essentially find themselves in a two-dimensional relationship to society and the state – a political-military and a civil-military one

[597] While the political-military relationship framework is precisely defined by constitutional and legal provisions that determine the integration of the armed forces into the political system and the mechanisms for their democratic control, the civil-military aspect refers to the socio-political and cultural factors that significantly influence the relationship between the armed forces and society

[598] Understandably, the area of civil-military relations offers the armed forces far more opportunities for influence and shaping policy than the essentially determined area of political-military relations, which, however, should also be exploited insofar as political decisions in a democracy depend significantly on social developments and values

[599] The framework conditions for the development of security and armed forces in democratic societies and the political decisions required for this are formed in particular by those parameters that can be summarized under the term functional and societal imperative

[600] The functional imperative refers to the security policy environment as well as the risk, danger and threat picture, as it results primarily from the international environment with its political, economic, social and cultural fields of relationship

[601] In contrast, the societal imperative encompasses all social, political and cultural factors that affect the relationship between the armed forces and society and the attitudes of politicians and the public towards issues of security and defence

[602] Both imperatives do not stand in isolation from one another, but are inextricably linked for a successful security policy and thus adequate integration of the armed forces into the political and social environment

[603] The functional requirements arising from the international strategic environment result in the demand for the functionality of security policy and its instruments, including the armed forces

[604] The functional imperative therefore represents the factual level of security policy, which in open social systems must now be transferred to the meaning level and transported there, as a social imperative, so to speak

[605] In open societies, every system requires a fundamentally affirmative civil society environment that fundamentally recognizes and supports the existence, goals, and procedures of this organization as necessary

[606] In this context, it is important to consider the special phenomenon that armed forces essentially perform an emergency function for society

[607] In contrast to other organizations that legitimize themselves in a clear way for citizens on a daily basis (such as medical services or the police), what the armed forces do is not a matter of routine

[608] Fortunately, neither flood disasters nor armed conflicts occur on a daily basis, but this also deprives armed forces of the opportunity to make their efficiency performance immediately and permanently visible to society

[609] In conveying meaning in security policy and military contexts, it is therefore always a matter of making the productivity and benefit of the military organization for society conceivable in the form of abstract hypothetical projections directed towards future eventualities or comparative analogies

[610] Armed forces in functional transformation

[611] The changed security policy environment is characterized by the fact that a classic military threat no longer exists

[612] These are being replaced by subconventional and also asymmetric forms of conflict, which are leading to a significant reduction in the importance of classical military security

[613] The disappearance of the classic threat, a state of external hostility, has corresponding effects on the security concepts and the identity of the armed forces

[614] The new task profile – peace missions, humanitarian interventions, preventive/acute de-escalation of conflicts – requires multifunctionality and multi-options of armed forces, mostly outside their own national territory

[615] This leads to quantitative disarmament within the armed forces in the sense of drastic reductions in personnel strengths and qualitative upgrades in terms of technological and professional competence

[616] Furthermore, security challenges must be increasingly addressed through the interaction of civilian and military forces, which is why increased cooperation between civilian and military forces can be observed as a further feature of the functional transformation of armed forces

[617] However, we must also warn against the often-made conclusion that the absence of a classic military threat means that armed forces are dispensable

[618] Notwithstanding the aforementioned quantitative disarmament, armed forces offer significant peace benefits to society, which are reflected in the availability of human and material resources, rapid response capacity, streamlined organization, and technical expertise that no other organization can contribute to security efforts

[619] The objective necessity to maintain military capacities is therefore present even if there is no immediate military threat

[620] White Paper 2004 Analysis Balance Sheet Perspectives

[621] Armed forces in social transformation

[622] From the perspective of the societal imperative, there are impacts on the armed forces in their transformation process, which creates additional and specific pressure for change

[623] Due to social change, society's understanding of security is changing

[624] Although terrorist attacks or ecological disasters are increasingly entering public consciousness, the subjective sense of security, such as a secure job, family security or an appropriate income, dominates the population's sense of security

[625] As a result, however, the provision of external security by the military loses social relevance

[626] Furthermore, the societal tendency towards individualization and pluralization does not necessarily make the military environment with its collective demands attractive

[627] In connection with individualization, the phenomenon of professionalization and specialization in all areas of society must also be addressed

[628] This leads to a reduced acceptance of the concept of conscription and to the demand for professionalization of the armed forces in order to be able to meet the new requirements of the military

[629] In addition, a key characteristic of not only postmodern civil society is the demand for non-violent peacemaking, since violence as a means of conflict resolution is fundamentally outlawed in civil society

[630] Furthermore, the increased level of education and information in society and the associated need for information and communication represent an additional, albeit not really new, challenge for the armed forces

[631] All institutions of society and state, including the armed forces, are increasingly being critically scrutinized and are faced with a permanent need for legitimacy

[632] Legitimacy and acceptance

[633] Under the critical conditions of modern information and knowledge societies, organizations must be functionally and morally grounded and derive from this justification the legitimacy and recognition of their actions

[634] As already mentioned, an organization requires an affirmative, positive civil society environment that fundamentally recognizes and supports the existence, goals and procedures of this organization as necessary

[635] While the Austrian Armed Forces have previously been able to derive their legitimacy from national defense and the preservation of territorial integrity, new sources of legitimacy are required in the context of the changing understanding of security

[636] These must enable the military to find new functional and moral justifications for its contribution to the common good of the state in the complex security scenario of the globalization age

[637] The question is therefore

[638] How can social acceptance of the purpose and functionality of the armed forces be achieved in light of the drastically changed conditions in the security policy environment? If acceptance is understood as the extent, the degree of actual agreement with an institution and its actions or intentions, then acceptance exists when the overwhelming majority of the population recognizes the armed forces, along with their assigned tasks, goals, and procedures, as legitimate and indispensable for the common good of society

[639] A particular challenge in this regard is the integration of the population's subjective, individual perception of security and threat with the objective, state security analysis

[640] Concept of security

[641] In political terms, the concept of security is understood as the absence of or protection from threats that can affect the existence and well-being of a people, as well as its social stability and political peace

[642] The dominance of non-military threats and security risks, which now characterise the international scenario, has led to an expanded concept of security, which makes security as a prerequisite for peaceful coexistence (of people and states) dependent on interdependencies between aspects of external and internal security

[643] In addition to political analysis, balance sheet perspectives and economic framework conditions, subjective risk and threat perceptions in society are crucial for security policy and thus for the acceptance of armed forces

[644] When dealing with insecurity, democratic societies therefore refer, on the one hand, to the "objective" security situation (as perceived by politicians and their security agencies) and, on the other hand, to the subjective feelings of security of the population

[645] Floods in the summer of 2002 only had a short-term impact on the sense of security of Austrians and hardly changed the long-term trend

[646] If we consider further survey results, it can be seen that the factors of uncertainty cited are primarily personal concerns such as the loss of family security, financial losses or the loss of a job

[647] Terrorism and international crime are considered to be the main threats to Austria

[648] the classic military threat is clearly fading into the background

[649] What is striking is that around a third of the Austrian population does not feel threatened at all

[650] Women generally feel less safe than men, but there is a growing tendency towards gender equality. While subjective perceptions of threat and security are mostly shaped by individual interests and value preferences, official state threat analysis attempts to largely eliminate subjectivity and individual influences

[651] This is achieved by moving away from assessments based solely on immediate impressions and through civil-military cooperation in security policy research and analysis

[652] According to the “Security Barometer” surveyed and published semi-annually by the Federal Chancellery (BKA) for 11 years now, the subjective individual perception of security in Austria remains at a consistently high level

[653] On a five-point scale, with 1 being very safe and 5 being very unsafe, the values are consistently in the upper range and have fluctuated only slightly between 1.84 and 2.20 since 1993. Perceived threats such as the terrorist attack of September 11, 2001, the Iraq War, and threats from natural disasters such as the avalanche disaster in Galtür in 1999 or the 2004 White Paper Analysis Balance Perspectives of specific differences have continued consistently in recent years

[654] The studies also clearly show that the subjective feeling of security increases with higher levels of education and income

[655] In relation to age, younger people feel somewhat safer than older people

[656] If one compares these data with surveys conducted by the European Union, they show that the Austrian population feels safer than average compared to the rest of the EU

[657] When asked about the tasks of the Austrian Armed Forces (ÖBH) according to the Defence Act, 91% of the population consider disaster relief to be an important and essential task for the ÖBH, but 85% consider military national defence to be almost as important

[658] The Austrians rate the assistance provided by the Austrian Armed Forces abroad as being significantly less important, at only 58%, although the Austrian Armed Forces' foreign missions enjoy relatively high acceptance among the population

[659] What is particularly worrying, however, is the significant difference in attitudes among the Austrian population regarding trust in the security forces

[660] While trust in the police and the military is roughly equal in the EU at 67% and 66% respectively, in Austria the police are trusted almost twice as much (84%) as the Austrian Armed Forces (47%

[661] Female soldiers in the Austrian Armed Forces

[662] The integration of women as soldiers into military organizations is a central feature of post-modern armed forces development

[663] This is due, on the one hand, to the new areas of responsibility and the associated professionalization of the armed forces, and, on the other hand, to the demand for a greater openness of the armed forces towards civilian values and societal concerns

[664] The opening of the military profession to female soldiers is primarily related to social equality trends and less to the immediate functional needs of the armed forces

[665] Since January 1998, it has been legally possible for women to pursue the profession of “soldier” in the Austrian Armed Forces

[666] Military service for women in Austria was defined as a training service, which is neither military service nor a service relationship, but rather a training relationship of its own kind, which serves the exclusive purpose of preparing the female soldier for employment as a temporary or professional military person

[667] Entry into military service takes place by submitting a voluntary application for training service and its acceptance by the responsible Army Personnel Office (HPA) after successful assessment of suitability (aptitude test

[668] The financial and social status of female soldiers corresponds to that of men subject to military service, although at the time of writing this article, significant changes are taking place in this regard, based on the recommendations of the Federal Army Reform Commission

[669] The idea is to adapt to international practices and also to measure the training of female soldiers not against the basic military service of conscripts but against comparable professional profiles (such as the police or customs guard

[670] The training service for female soldiers lasts 12 months

[671] In addition, women have the opportunity to join the militia on a voluntary basis, which allows for voluntary weapons training as well as foreign deployment service for women

[672] Special provisions govern the case of the soldier’s motherhood

[673] In the absence of an employment relationship, the female soldier is not entitled to parental leave during her training service

[674] However, she has the right to interrupt her training service due to maternity and to continue it without a new aptitude test within three years of the birth of the child

[675] Otherwise, the same maternity protection provisions apply as in the public sector

[676] In Austria, the number of female soldiers corresponds to approximately 0.7% of the total number of soldiers, which means that the proportion of female soldiers can be considered very low compared to other armies in general

[677] There may be many reasons why women in Austria are generally less willing to take advantage of this career opportunity

[678] However, a key factor is certainly the physical limits that the female soldier must meet before the actual training service begins, and which are considered to be above average in international comparison

[679] Combined with the low pay factor, the physical performance assessment prior to the start of training service is the primary reason for the lack of female applicants and the very high dropout rate among those interested. However, changes are currently being planned in this regard as well, which are intended to give female soldiers the opportunity to increase their physical performance, similar to that of conscripts, to a level required of soldiers during the course of their training service, under easier and more internationally comparable conditions

[680] For recruitment purposes and to prepare specifically for the entrance examination, preparatory weekends are offered to interested candidates on a voluntary basis

[681] Several times a year there are also taster and career days, which are intended to provide a more comprehensive picture of the Austrian Armed Forces career field

[682] As of December 2004, 253 women are serving as soldiers in the Austrian Armed Forces

[690] Austrian Security and Defense Policy 5.1 Aim and purpose of Austrian security policy Security in all its dimensions is a fundamental prerequisite for the existence and functioning of a constitutional democracy as well as for the economic well-being of society and its citizens

[691] Security policy is therefore a primary political task of every state

[692] It must be conceived and implemented as a comprehensive security policy under the current conditions

[693] Austria is committed to a policy of peace

[694] It therefore aims to prevent violent conflicts from arising in the first place

[695] It pursues a security policy based on the Charter of the United Nations and international agreements for the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms, such as the European Convention on Human Rights and the European Charter of Fundamental Rights, aimed at avoiding war and at peaceful coexistence between peoples

[696] The purpose of security policy is to ensure security for as many areas of a community as possible

[697] The security and defense doctrine deals in particular with those aspects of comprehensive security that are concerned with the protection of the state system as a whole and the protection of its citizens against large-scale threats

[698] This does not diminish the importance of other areas of security

[699] The Security and Defence Doctrine represents the guiding principle for Austria’s security policy

[700] Austria's vital security interests and the security interests pursued jointly with the EU form the basis of security policy

[701] This gives rise to the political-strategic objectives that are to be implemented through an overall government strategy as well as through sub-strategies in the respective policy areas

[702] The security situation of a European state can no longer be viewed in isolation

[703] Instabilities and threats in Europe and on the European periphery affect the security situation of all European states

[704] The new security policy challenges and risks cannot be met alone, but only through international cooperation and solidarity

[705] Austria's security and that of the EU are inextricably linked

[706] Today, Austria implements its security policy essentially within the framework of the EU

[707] An important aspect in connection with a comprehensive understanding of security is the recognition that security is not only the responsibility of the state, but of the entire population

[708] Great attention must therefore be paid to the development of a general security awareness

[709] Objectives and tasks of Austrian defence policy The essential foundations of the (current) Austrian defence policy are set out in the security and defence doctrine, the draft partial strategy and the government programme for the 21st century

[710] The aim of Austrian defence policy is to make a military contribution to protecting the population from threats and to safeguarding Austrian sovereignty, as well as to ensure, through military capacities commensurate with Austria's weight in the international community, a solidary participation in international military crisis prevention and crisis management that serves Austrian security interests

[711] Austrian defense policy encompasses all military measures to safeguard Austria's security interests

[712] It is embedded in the national strategy of comprehensive security provision

[713] It represents the implementation of the political guidelines of the security and defense doctrine

[714] The Federal Minister of Defence is responsible for implementing Austrian defence policy

[715] It has the following tasks:4 ¾ Participation in the national formulation of security policy objectives and measures within the framework of an interdepartmental leadership and planning process

[716] ¾ permanent assessment of the strategic situation for the purpose of early crisis detection and as a contribution to the leadership process of the top command in the national and multinational context, ¾ determination of the contribution of the BMLV and the Austrian Armed Forces within the framework of the national security strategy, analysis of the balance sheet

[717] Participation in the national determination of Austria’s forward-looking and event-related military contribution in the international context

[718] Formulating defense policy objectives as a political framework for military strategy and the mandate of the Federal Army, as well as the exercise of command authority through commanders, Shaping international defense policy cooperation and participating in confidence-and security-building measures as well as in arms control and WMD non-proliferation measures, Initiating and participating in shaping the legislative framework, providing financial resources, and ensuring the personnel, material, and organizational requirements for fulfilling military tasks in accordance with the Federal Constitutional Law (B-VG), the Defence Act 2001 (WG 2001), the Deployment Act (KSE-BVG), and the security and defense doctrine, Contributing to strengthening the institutions of the European Security and Defense Policy (ESDP), particularly with regard to increased responsibility of the defence ministers

[719] Regulation of fundamental issues of information, communication, education and research policy, insofar as they affect security or defense policy issues of the department

[720] Euro-strategic security

[721] The new risks, especially the threat of terrorism and the remaining conventional residual risk, which is generally considered to be low, can only be viewed in an internationally networked manner

[722] The expansion of the EU and NATO and the associated security structures have strengthened Europe as an area of stability

[723] Austria is geopolitically at the center of this development and its security will be increased as a result

[724] The territory of the Union as well as the immediate and wider geostrategic environment of the EU are of great importance in this regard

[725] Notwithstanding the high importance of cooperation within the UN, the OSCE and also with NATO through the Partnership for Peace, the primary framework for Austria's action in this area is the EU

[726] In view of the current comprehensive challenges and their assessable development, the establishment of a new transatlantic relationship is of particular importance

[727] A common defense of the EU without sufficient consideration of the interests of the USA is to be considered very unlikely, even in the long term

[728] White Paper 2004 Analysis Balance Sheet

[729] For the EU, it is important, among other things, to become more capable of action in the military field and to become a credible partner

[730] By accelerating the development of the ESDP, the EU has responded to the new challenges

[731] The starting point for this is the European Security Strategy, which clearly identifies the threats of the 21st century

[732] The acceptance of the expanded Petersberg range of tasks reflects the Union's recognition that it must truly address current and foreseeable security policy challenges comprehensively

[733] For Austria, this means that, against the background of common European defense, the ability to participate in militarily demanding missions in the sense of safeguarding the interests of the EU should become the essential long-term goal of defense policy

[734] This is primarily a qualitative objective that is closely linked to the development of common EU capacities

[735] Maximum flexibility of the security policy framework

[736] is of particular importance here

[737] The legal and political conditions in Austria should enable participation in the broadest possible spectrum of forms of international crisis management

[738] Remaining national tasks from a strategic perspective

[739] The protection of the population is the primary goal of Austrian defense policy

[740] This protection is increasingly being ensured at an international, particularly European, level

[741] Ensuring the protection and safeguarding of the basic functions of the state remain essential tasks to be performed on Austrian territory

[742] These can be carried out as a military operation or as an assistance service, possibly with the involvement of international support forces

[743] These national tasks are also becoming increasingly important as a prerequisite for Austria’s ability to participate in international tasks

[744] Only if the Austrian population's need for protection is met and the conditions for the smooth functioning of state processes are met can Austria be a reliable partner in international crisis management and, in the long term, in a common defense

[745] However, the ability to carry out national tasks must be coordinated internationally to a greater extent, so that the possibility is created of putting the resources provided for national tasks at the service of European solidarity, if necessary

[746] The international framework of defense policy Austria's ability to safeguard its interests at the international level is largely determined by the quality of its military contributions to international crisis management

[747] What is crucial here is the scope for action that the military instrument gives the political leadership in its international engagement

[748] This scope for action includes not only the ability to contribute quickly, flexibly and qualitatively to the broadest possible spectrum of international crisis management, but also, together with other responsible parties, to ensure the functionality of the state and the protection of the population

[749] This range of tasks is complex and includes civilian and military aspects that must complement each other flexibly

[750] The basic prerequisite for this is and remains the constant observation and updating of the strategic situation picture

[751] International cooperation for European security EU

[752] The principles of the ESDP were established and further developed in a series of decisions of the European Council (EC), starting with the Cologne Council in June

[753] The political foundation was laid at the British-French summit in St. Malo on 3 and 4 December

[754] The core point of the St. Malo agreement, which must be seen against the backdrop of the Kosovo crisis, was that NATO should continue to be the framework for collective defense, but that the EU must have the capacity for military crisis management in order to fully assume its role on the international stage

[755] At the Helsinki European Council in December 1999, the military capability goals (Headline Goal) to be achieved by 2003 were set at 60,000 troops, deployable within two months and with a one-year sustainability capability

[756] In addition to military crisis management, civilian crisis management and conflict prevention were identified and further developed as separate areas – not least due to the insistence of the non-aligned

[757] Specific capability targets were set for civilian crisis management (including 5,000 police officers

[758] The proposed contributions of individual Member States to the civilian and military capability objectives are voluntary

[759] The actual provision of personnel and resources for a specific operation is a separate decision taken by each Member State sovereignly and in accordance with its national regulations

[760] The Austrian contribution to the military capability objective consists of an infantry battalion for peace enforcement, an infantry battalion for peacekeeping, and various special forces (a total of approximately 1,500 soldiers

[761] For civilian capabilities, Austria provides 110 police officers, 10 prison guards, and civil and disaster protection forces

[762] After the Helsinki Headline Goal was at least quantitatively achieved by 2003 and the operationality of the ESDP was generally ensured, a new list of objectives was adopted with the target date of 2010 (Headline Goal

[766] At the same time, the EU should have the ability to carry out several operations simultaneously

[767] In order to ensure the ability to act within the framework of the ESDP, the following new Council structures were installed in the period up to June 2001 with the decision of the European Council in Helsinki in 1999: PSC Political and Security Committee

[768] The PSC consists of national representatives at ambassadorial level and monitors the international situation in the area of CFSP

[769] It also contributes to the development of new strategies and monitors their implementation

[770] Under the supervision of the Council of the European Union, the PSC ensures political control and strategic direction of crisis management actions

[771] The work of the PSC is supported by the Political-Military Affairs Working Party, the Committee on Civilian Aspects of Crisis Management (Civil Crisis Management Committee/CCMK), the EU Military Committee (EUMC) and the EU Military Staff (EUMS

[772] EUMC (European Military Committee) consists of the Chiefs of Staff of the armed forces of all Member States, represented by their military delegates in Brussels

[773] He directs all military activities within the Union

[774] EUMS EU Military Staff, with currently around officers (four of whom are from Austria), is responsible for the ESDP, especially for the conduct of EU-led military crisis management operations

[775] The EUMS is responsible for early warning, situation assessment and strategic planning with regard to the Petersberg tasks, including the determination of the respective European national and multinational

[776] Not only has the ESDP's mandate been functionally expanded, but its area of operation has also been extended

[777] In June 2003, the EU's first independent operation (Artemis) was carried out in Africa within the framework of a mandate

[778] At the same time, the EU remained heavily involved in the Balkans, particularly in Bosnia and Herzegovina. On January 1, 2003, the EU took over the previously UN-led Police Mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina (EUPM – roughly translated as "police officers") as its first ESDP operation

[779] Following the Berlin Plus agreement with NATO, the EU took over the NATO mission in Macedonia (Operation Concordia – about 500 soldiers) on 31 March

[784] Cooperation with NATO
