[3801] In its government programme of 3 February 2000, the Federal Government decided to restructure security and defence policy in the broadest possible national consensus and to adapt it to the changed conditions in the environment

[3802] Accordingly, at its meeting in May 2000 (item 16 of Protocol 14), the Council of Ministers decided, at the request of the Federal Minister of Defence, to set up a commission to develop a new Austrian security and defence doctrine

[3803] Subsequently, the analytical part of the security and defense doctrine was developed at expert level

[3804] This part of the analysis was acknowledged by the Council of Ministers on 23 January 2001 (item 39 of Protocol 44) and forwarded to the National Council for consideration

[3805] After preliminary discussions in a subcommittee of the National Defence Committee, during which no consensus could be reached, the governing parties in the National Defence Committee decided on 7 December 2001 by a majority to recommend that the plenary session of the National Council take note of the summary report on the status of the negotiations

[3806] In addition, a motion for a resolution submitted by the governing parties concerning a new Austrian security and defense doctrine was adopted

[3807] On 12 December 2001, the National Council then decided by a majority to take note of the report submitted by the Federal Government on the security and defence doctrine (analytical part) and to adopt the resolution on a new Austrian security and defence doctrine attached in the annex

[3808] This resolution of the National Council provides, for the first time since the defence doctrine adopted by the National Council on 10 June 1975, a fundamental political guideline for the design of Austrian security policy

[3809] The resolution takes account of new developments in security policy and is based in particular on the following fundamental principles

[3810] Austrian security policy is based on the principle of comprehensive security, which attaches appropriate importance to both military and non-military aspects of security

[3811] The principle of preventive security replaces the threat response concept

[3812] Active participation in international conflict prevention and crisis management measures is an important part of Austria's security policy

[3813] The principle of European solidarity replaces the concept of an autonomous security policy

[3814] Austria’s security and that of the EU are inextricably linked

[3815] The new security policy challenges and risks cannot be overcome alone but only through international cooperation based on solidarity

[3816] Based on the expert draft of the analysis section of the security and defense doctrine, the National Council's resolution is based on general considerations, which describe in particular the security policy paradigm shift in Europe, the security policy risks and threats, the security situation in Austria, the role of international organizations and Austria's solidarity based participation, as well as the development from neutrality to solidarity

[3817] In light of these considerations, the resolution lists general recommendations as well as recommendations on the foreign policy aspects of security policy, defence policy and internal security

[3818] On the basis of these recommendations on security and defence policy contained in the resolution, the National Council requests the Federal Government to develop partial strategies for all areas relevant to security policy

[3819] The sub-strategies should in particular contain those measures necessary to implement the recommendations

[3820] These sub-strategies should be continuously reviewed, coordinated and, if necessary, adapted in accordance with the international framework

[3821] They should relate in particular to the areas of foreign policy, defence policy and internal security

[3822] In addition, sub-strategies will be developed in the areas of economic, agricultural, transport, infrastructure and financial policy, as well as education and information policy

[3823] The federal ministries responsible for the individual sub-strategies should therefore draw up corresponding sub-strategies by the end of September 2002 at the latest, based on the resolution on the Austrian security and defence doctrine adopted by the National Council, so that an agreed overall strategy can be drawn up by the end of December

[3824] The existing processes and structures will have to be reviewed with a view to increasing efficiency and exploiting synergies

[3825] The Federal Law of 16 November 2001, BGBl

[3826] The National Security Council established by Article I, No. 122, is requested to assume the political coordination of the implementation of the measures contained in the National Council’s resolution concerning a new Austrian security and defence doctrine and to submit a report on the status of implementation to the Federal Government at least once a year

[3827] Security and Defence Doctrine General Considerations Based on the expert draft of the analysis section of the Security and Defence Doctrine (III-87 dB), which was acknowledged by the Federal Government on 23 January 2001 and submitted to the National Council for consultation, the following conclusions arise: Security in all its dimensions is a basic prerequisite for the existence and functioning of a constitutional democracy as well as for the economic well-being of society and its citizens

[3828] Security policy is therefore a primary political task of every state

[3829] It must be conceived and implemented as a comprehensive security policy under today's conditions

[3830] Austria is committed to a policy of peace

[3831] It therefore aims to prevent violent conflicts from arising in the first place

[3832] It therefore pursues a security policy based on the Charter of the United Nations and international agreements for the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms, such as the European Convention on Human Rights and the European Charter of Fundamental Rights, aimed at avoiding war and promoting peaceful coexistence between peoples

[3833] The purpose of security policy is to ensure security for as many areas of a community as possible

[3834] The security and defense doctrine deals in particular with those aspects of comprehensive security that are concerned with the protection of the state system as a whole and the protection of its citizens against large-scale threats

[3835] This does not diminish the importance of other areas of security

[3836] The Security and Defence Doctrine represents the guiding principle for Austria’s security policy

[3837] Austria's vital security interests and the security interests pursued jointly with the EU form the basis of security policy

[3838] This gives rise to the political-strategic objectives that are to be implemented through an overall government strategy as well as through sub-strategies in the respective policy areas

[3839] The security situation of a European state can no longer be viewed in isolation

[3840] Instabilities and threats in Europe or on the European periphery affect the security situation of all European states

[3841] The new security policy challenges and risks cannot be addressed alone but only through international cooperation based on solidarity

[3842] Austria’s security and that of the EU are inextricably linked

[3843] Today, Austria implements its security policy essentially within the framework of the EU

[3844] An important aspect of a comprehensive understanding of security is the recognition that security is not only the responsibility of the state, but of the entire population

[3845] Great attention must therefore be paid to developing a general awareness of security

[3846] Security policy paradigm shift in Europe

[3847] The changes in the global political situation that occurred after the end of the Cold War have led to a fundamental change in European security policy

[3848] A paradigm shift in security policy has taken place in Europe

[3849] This process, which began with the end of the Cold War, led from a military balance and deterrence mentality to an understanding of comprehensive, cooperative security

[3850] The bipolar order with a relatively stable and therefore manageable constellation of power and threats was replaced by a new complexity of the world order and new security policy challenges

[3851] The global security situation is characterized by a growing number of state and, above all, non-state actors, some of which are not integrated into the traditional political order and operate outside of applicable legal norms

[3852] The security situation is therefore becoming increasingly complex and its development less predictable

[3853] Physical distance from conflict zones no longer provides sufficient protection

[3854] Currently, there are no discernible aggressive political intentions in Europe, nor is there sufficient military potential for strategic offensive operations

[3855] However, a responsible security policy must be prepared for the possibility that political intentions and constellations may change

[3856] A modern and future-oriented security policy is based on preventing the emergence of risks and threats through preventive measures

[3857] It is primarily oriented towards how Europe can and must be shaped so that threats do not arise in the first place

[3858] The instruments of security policy action have been given new emphasis

[3859] In particular, the following cooperation and design instruments are used today

[3860] Political, military, police, intelligence, economic, social, educational, cultural, information and communication policy, ecological, and internal security. Peace and stability in Europe are based on the cooperation of European states in various security organizations

[3861] The zone of high stability already formed by the EU and NATO will be gradually extended through the enlargement process to include those states that meet the requirements for joining these two organisations

[3862] The security policy development of the EU and NATO will be of particular importance for the future of Europe

[3863] Other important factors will be the US engagement in Europe and the development of Russia's security relations with the EU and NATO

[3864] The individual states are the decision-makers and the key actors in security policy

[3865] The final decision on security policy issues lies with the democratically legitimized national political authorities

[3866] Security policy risks and dangers replace a clear threat picture

[3867] Instead of a clearly identifiable threat picture like during the Cold War, a complex mixture of dangers and risks has emerged

[3868] The origins of this can lie in the political, economic, military, social, ecological, cultural religious and information technology areas

[3869] From today's perspective, interstate wars in Western Europe can be ruled out for the foreseeable future

[3870] However, in the unstable regions of Europe and its periphery, the risk of armed conflicts remains

[3871] In particular, if economic and political stabilisation measures fail, the possibility of escalation of political disputes and even armed conflict must be taken into account

[3872] In the medium to long term, threats from the spillover of armed conflicts from regions bordering Europe cannot be ruled out

[3873] In the event of fundamentally changed political intentions, a residual military risk must also be taken into account

[3874] This is currently considered to be low due to the deterrent effect exerted by NATO

[3875] Other forms of threat, however, are increasing

[3876] The most important global security challenges are the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, terrorism directed by states or interest groups and operating internationally, organized crime, destabilizing arms developments, ethnic conflicts, political fragmentation phenomena, totalitarian ideologies and fundamentalist religions, population development and migration, energy and resource problems, food problems, and environmental threats

[3877] International terrorism in all its forms is a serious security problem for Western society

[3878] The comprehensive understanding of security includes the following basic strategies: promotion, safeguarding and restoration of peace and stability as well as individual/collective self-defense

[3879] The principle is: “As much cooperative peacebuilding as possible and only as much coercive action as necessary.”

[3880] The use of military coercive force remains a means of last resort and may only be used in accordance with the principles of the United Nations

[3881] Austria's security situation is currently characterized by a number of positive circumstances

[3882] These include, in particular, internal stability based on the rule of law, democracy and economic prosperity, Austria's integration into the solidarity community of the EU and the good relations with its neighbouring countries

[3883] The EU and NATO enlargement processes also have positive effects on Austria’s geopolitical situation

[3884] An existence-threatening aggression against Austria with conventional armed forces is only conceivable in the event of a fundamental change in the political situation in Europe; according to current military-strategic assessments, such a change would require a lead time of seven to ten years

[3885] Despite the current low probability, it cannot be ruled out

[3886] In the area of internal security, it can be stated that the stable economic, social and political conditions in Austria have not allowed extremist phenomena that pose a serious threat to state security to emerge in recent years

[3887] There is currently no danger of domestically motivated political terrorism in Austria

[3888] Nevertheless, there are potential risks and dangers that could quickly and decisively change Austria’s security situation

[3889] Due to the complex and cross-border threat and risk contexts, physical distance from crisis areas no longer provides sufficient protection

[3890] Therefore, conflicts that arise outside of consolidated Europe can also have negative repercussions for Austria

[3891] These include, in particular, international terrorism, arms, drug and human trafficking, migration flows based on a variety of motives, environmental disasters and crises in the economic and financial sectors

[3892] These risks can be countered through preventive measures on the ground, including comprehensive measures of political and economic support, assistance in building democratic and constitutional structures, and international military presence on the ground

[3893] Modern societies are particularly vulnerable in the information sector

[3894] This affects both the military and the civilian sector and, increasingly, the economy (industrial and technological espionage

[3895] Due to the progressive development and availability of long-range air warfare capabilities, especially ballistic missiles and cruise missiles, a military threat to Austria may arise from regions outside Europe within just a few years

[3896] Furthermore, the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction can lead to new threats for Austria, despite appropriate non-proliferation regimes

[3897] Austria is also confronted with the negative effects of globalization, particularly in the form of organized crime and international terrorism, but also illegal migration

[3898] Dangers such as subversive attacks on strategically important infrastructure, terrorist attacks or the threat of blackmail to enforce certain political goals are becoming increasingly important in conjunction with the availability of new means of deployment (especially weapons of mass destruction and information technology

[3899] Such threats can come from both state and non-state actors, such as terrorist movements, organized crime groups, sects, but also from individual perpetrators

[3900] What is characteristic of such threats is that they usually occur unexpectedly and without warning

[3901] Natural, technical or ecological disasters as well as epidemic diseases are also considered to be significant risk and hazard potentials

[3902] These include, in particular, accidents in nuclear power plants, which can have widespread effects

[3903] Role of international organizations and Austria's solidarity-based participation Security and stability can best be ensured today through the cooperation of institutions that functionally complement and mutually support each other

[3904] These include the United Nations and, in the European and transatlantic context, in particular the EU, NATO with the Partnership for Peace (PfP) it established and the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council (EAPC), as well as the OSCE and the Council of Europe

[3905] Active participation in international conflict prevention and crisis management measures is an important part of Austria's security policy

[3906] Austria is therefore also striving to continuously improve its crisis management capacities in the civilian and military sectors

[3907] Austria attaches central importance to the role of the United Nations in maintaining world peace and international security

[3908] Participation in UN peacekeeping operations has been one of the focal points of Austria's engagement in the world organization since the Congo mission in

[3909] Since 1960, approximately 40,000 members of the Austrian Armed Forces have participated in United Nations-authorized operations

[3910] Austria's role in UN peacekeeping missions has evolved in the 1990s

[3911] Since then, Austria has also participated in peacekeeping operations, including with combat troops since

[3912] These are UN-authorized missions that are carried out under the operational leadership of NATO or a "lead nation

[3913] Austria plays an equally active role in the OSCE as it did in the Conference for Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE), its predecessor institution

[3914] During the Cold War, Austria was particularly interested in understanding and cooperation between East and West due to its geographical location

[3915] After the fall of the Iron Curtain, Austria has a natural interest in stabilizing conditions in the east of the European continent

[3916] The OSCE, which is based on a comprehensive cooperative security concept, currently offers 55 states in Europe, North America and Central Asia a forum for equal cooperation

[3917] It makes an important contribution to stability in Europe and thus to Austrian security

[3918] Austria supports a further strengthening of the OSCE, particularly in the areas of early warning, conflict prevention, civilian crisis management and post-conflict rehabilitation

[3919] A key motivation for Austria’s accession to the EU was its membership in the European stability zone

[3920] From the outset, European integration was seen as a work of peace and thus as a security policy concept

[3921] The current EU enlargement process can therefore also bring benefits from a security policy perspective

[3922] Austria joined the EU without any reservation of neutrality

[3923] Upon ratification of the Austrian Accession Treaty, Article 23f was inserted into the Federal Constitution, which stipulates that participation in the Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP) is not constitutionally restricted by the Neutrality Act

[3924] At the Helsinki European Council in December 1999, it was decided that the EU should be given credible military capabilities and efficient decision-making structures so that it can conduct crisis management operations autonomously in the future

[3925] Austria fully supports the dynamic development of the Common European Security and Defence Policy (CESDP

[3926] Austria is thus demonstrating its determination to participate on an equal footing and in solidarity in all areas of European security and defence

[3927] Austria will make an adequate contribution to the EU’s military and civilian capabilities

[3928] Europe’s security depends primarily on the functioning of the EU and NATO

[3929] Today, NATO presents itself not as a mere classic military alliance, but as a comprehensive security community based on democratic values, which, through its stability-oriented policies, makes a decisive contribution to peace and security worldwide

[3930] Austria supports close and trusting cooperation between the EU and NATO

[3931] In a framework document signed in February 1995, Austria expressed its intention to work towards the realisation of the objectives underlying the Partnership for Peace (PfP

[3932] According to the “Austrian Introductory Document” of May 1995, cooperation with NATO and the PfP participants includes in particular cooperation in peacekeeping

[3933] Operations, humanitarian and disaster relief, and search and rescue operations

[3934] As a PfP partner, Austria participated in the NATO-led multinational peace operation in Bosnia and Herzegovina (IFOR/SFOR) from 1995 to

[3935] Austria has been participating in the Kosovo Force (KFOR) since autumn

[3936] Since 1997, the “deepened PfP” has provided all partners with the opportunity to establish interoperability across the entire spectrum of peace support measures, including peace enforcement through combat operations

[3937] This aligned the spectrum of PfP peace support measures with that of the Petersberg missions

[3938] Austria also actively participates in the work of the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council (EAPC), the PfP’s political consultation forum

[3939] The EAPC serves to discuss a wide range of political and security-related issues

[3940] Based on a tailor-made cooperation program, Austria has initiated a bilateral dialogue on security policy issues with NATO and intensified its cooperation with NATO in the civil and military fields

[3941] The Council of Europe, to which almost all European states now belong, is the central institution for safeguarding human rights and fundamental freedoms, the rule of law and democracy

[3942] All Member States are obliged to comply with the European Convention on Human Rights; its provisions are enforceable before the European Court of Human Rights

[3943] The Council of Europe has a direct security policy function in crisis prevention and crisis rehabilitation

[3944] All efforts to bring the new Council of Europe states in the east of the European continent closer to the high standards of this organization are strongly supported by Austria, as they serve stability in Europe

[3945] From neutrality to solidarity

[3946] When the Austrian National Council passed the Federal Constitutional Law on Austrian Neutrality on 26 October 1955, it was clear that Austrian neutrality was modeled on that of Switzerland

[3947] However, Austrian neutrality soon differed from that of Switzerland: Austria joined the United Nations as early as December

[3948] In its relationship with the United Nations, Austria assumed until 1990 that the world organization was obliged to respect Austria's permanent neutrality and would therefore never use Austria to take coercive measures in a military conflict between third states

[3949] However, in the wake of the Gulf War of 1991, the legal opinion prevailed in Austria that the obligations under the Charter of the United Nations take precedence over the obligation of neutrality

[3950] This means that classic neutrality based on the Swiss model no longer exists

[3951] With its accession to the European Union in 1995, Austria adopted its entire legal and political acquis, which at that time already included the Treaty of Maastricht and its provisions on the Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP

[3952] Article J.4 of this Treaty opened up the prospect of a common defence policy which could, in due course, lead to a common defence

[3953] A provision (Article 23f) was included in the Federal Constitution to ensure that participation in the CFSP is not restricted by the Neutrality Act

[3954] The effectiveness of the Neutrality Act was thus further limited

[3955] Following the ratification of the Treaty of Amsterdam, the National Council passed a further constitutional amendment in 1998, according to which Austria can participate in the entire spectrum of the so-called Petersberg tasks, which also include combat missions in crisis management, including peace-making measures

[3956] Such participation is possible due to an EU decision

[3957] This development shows that Austria has, at the latest through its unconditional participation in the EU's Common Foreign and Security Policy, permanently changed its status of permanent neutrality under international law

[3958] In international comparison, Austria’s status under international law is therefore not that of a neutral state, but rather that of a non-aligned state

[3959] Austria decides sovereignly on the future development of its security policy

[3960] However, the better it is integrated into the international security architecture, the more efficiently it can implement its security interests and peace policy goals and contribute to creating a stable and peaceful environment

[3961] The Federal Government is requested to shape Austria’s security policy in particular according to the following principles: Austria’s comprehensive security policy should be shaped according to the following general principles

[3962] The Austrian population should be comprehensively and continuously informed about the security situation at home and abroad

[3963] This is an essential prerequisite for developing and maintaining a broad awareness of security needs

[3964] A National Security Council is intended to advise the Federal Government and the individual Federal Ministers on all fundamental matters of foreign, security and defence policy

[3965] To support the National Security Council, a Secretariat, together with liaison officers in the departments most affected, will evaluate and advise on these matters and prepare the Council's meetings

[3966] The European cooperation in intelligence information exchange that has already been initiated is to be intensified

[3967] At the same time, effective parliamentary oversight must be ensured to protect citizens' privacy and democratic achievements and rights

[3968] Comprehensive national defense must be further developed into a system of comprehensive security provision by focusing on new risks and threats and adapting legal provisions

[3969] Disaster relief in an international context has a historically grown significance for Austria

[3970] Austria has taken on an internationally respected pioneering role in this area and should continue to expand this

[3971] In order to improve the ability to cooperate between national and international aid and relief organizations, an integrated and coordinated training program is to be created that builds on existing civilian and military training facilities

[3972] The field of security policy research must be expanded in order to obtain a comprehensive picture of security and defense policy issues

[3973] To this end, close cooperation and networking between relevant organisations and institutions at home and abroad should be sought

[3974] In order to acquire and impart comprehensive security policy expertise, a postgraduate strategic leadership course for decision-makers in politics, business, administration and the military should be introduced

[3975] Austria should exploit opportunities for regional security policy cooperation with neighboring countries and other interested states

[3976] The availability of vital resources (such as food, energy and raw materials) as well as the protection of strategic infrastructure (such as communications and transport) should be ensured

[3981] Supporting developing world countries in their efforts towards economic, social, democratic and ecological development

[3982] Improving international environmental protection (including the Rio Process

[3985] Ongoing balancing of interests with EU partners to ensure the best possible implementation of Austrian interests within the EU

[3986] Development of a partnership with like-minded states linked by common regional interests (Regional Partnership concept

[4038] A secure Europe in a better world Brussels, 12 December 2003 Introduction

[4039] Never before has Europe been so prosperous, so safe and so free

[4040] The violence of the first half of the century has given way to a period of peace and stability unprecedented in European history

[4041] The creation of the European Union is at the heart of this development

[4042] It has changed the relations between our countries and the lives of our citizens

[4043] The European states have committed themselves to settling disputes peacefully and to cooperating in common institutions

[4044] Over time, the rule of law and democracy have become more and more prevalent, and authoritarian regimes have become insecure, stable, and dynamic democracies

[4045] Successive enlargements make the vision of a united and peaceful continent a reality

[4046] The United States has made a decisive contribution to the European unification process and to European security, particularly within NATO

[4047] Since the end of the Cold War, the United States has been the dominant military actor

[4048] Nevertheless, no country is capable of solving today’s complex problems alone

[4049] As far as European security is concerned, there are still threats and challenges

[4050] The outbreak of conflict in the Balkans has once again shown us that war has not disappeared from our continent

[4051] In the last decade, no region of the world has been spared from armed conflict

[4052] In most cases, these conflicts were intrastate rather than interstate in nature, and most of the victims were civilians

[4053] As an association of 25 states with over 450 million inhabitants, which generate a quarter of the world's gross national product (GNP), the European Union, which also has a comprehensive range of instruments at its disposal, is inevitably a global actor
